claim: Type III CRISPR systems detect foreign RNA and activate the cyclase domain of the Cas10 subunit, generating cyclic oligoadenylate (cOA) molecules.
source: Type III CRISPR systems detect foreign RNA and activate the cyclase domain of the Cas10 subunit, generating cyclic oligoadenylate (cOA) molecules that act as a second messenger to signal infection, activating nucleases that degrade the nucleic acid of both invader and host.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on type III CRISPR systems and their mechanism of action.

claim: Cyclic oligoadenylate molecules act as a second messenger to signal infection.
source: Type III CRISPR systems detect foreign RNA and activate the cyclase domain of the Cas10 subunit, generating cyclic oligoadenylate (cOA) molecules that act as a second messenger to signal infection, activating nucleases that degrade the nucleic acid of both invader and host.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cOA function in type III CRISPR systems.

claim: Cyclic oligoadenylate activates nucleases that degrade the nucleic acid of both invader and host.
source: Type III CRISPR systems detect foreign RNA and activate the cyclase domain of the Cas10 subunit, generating cyclic oligoadenylate (cOA) molecules that act as a second messenger to signal infection, activating nucleases that degrade the nucleic acid of both invader and host.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations about cOA-activated nucleases.

claim: Activation of the anti-viral state can lead to dormancy or cell death.
source: This can lead to dormancy or cell death; to avoid this, cells need a way to remove cOA from the cell once a viral infection has been defeated.
evidence: This is supported by citations and established knowledge about collateral damage from type III CRISPR systems.

claim: Cells need a mechanism to remove cOA from the cell once a viral infection has been defeated.
source: This can lead to dormancy or cell death; to avoid this, cells need a way to remove cOA from the cell once a viral infection has been defeated.
evidence: This is an inference based on the need to avoid cell death after infection clearance.

claim: Enzymes specialized for removing cOA are known as ring nucleases.
source: Enzymes specialised for this task are known as ring nucleases, but are limited in their distribution.
evidence: This is established nomenclature in the field.

claim: Ring nucleases are limited in their distribution.
source: Enzymes specialised for this task are known as ring nucleases, but are limited in their distribution.
evidence: This is supported by knowledge of the distribution of ring nucleases across organisms.

claim: Csx3 is a ring nuclease that rapidly degrades cyclic tetra-adenylate (cA4).
source: Here, we demonstrate that the widespread CRISPR associated protein Csx3, previously described as an RNA deadenylase, is a ring nuclease that rapidly degrades cyclic tetra-adenylate (cA4).
evidence: This is the primary finding of the manuscript, supported by experimental data presented in the figures.

claim: Csx3 was previously described as an RNA deadenylase.
source: Here, we demonstrate that the widespread CRISPR associated protein Csx3, previously described as an RNA deadenylase, is a ring nuclease that rapidly degrades cyclic tetra-adenylate (cA4).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Yan et al., 2015).

claim: Csx3 has an unusual cooperative reaction mechanism involving an active site that spans the interface between two dimers.
source: The enzyme has an unusual cooperative reaction mechanism involving an active site that spans the interface between two dimers, sandwiching the cA4 substrate.
evidence: This is supported by structural and biochemical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The active site of Csx3 sandwiches the cA4 substrate between two dimers.
source: The enzyme has an unusual cooperative reaction mechanism involving an active site that spans the interface between two dimers, sandwiching the cA4 substrate.
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure showing cA4 bound between dimers.

claim: The proposed name for the Csx3 family is Crn3 (CRISPR associated ring nuclease 3).
source: We propose the name Crn3 (CRISPR associated ring nuclease 3) for the Csx3 family.
evidence: This is a nomenclature proposal based on the functional characterization.

claim: Type III CRISPR systems are widespread in archaea and found in many bacteria.
source: Type III CRISPR systems are widespread in archaea and found in many bacteria (Makarova et al., 2011), including the human pathogen Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Grüschow et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on CRISPR distribution.

claim: Type III CRISPR systems are found in Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
source: Type III CRISPR systems are widespread in archaea and found in many bacteria (Makarova et al., 2011), including the human pathogen Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Grüschow et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grüschow et al., 2019.

claim: Type III effectors utilize a Cas7 backbone subunit to bind CRISPR RNA (crRNA).
source: Type III effectors utilise a Cas7 backbone subunit to bind CRISPR RNA (crRNA) (Rouillon et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rouillon et al., 2013.

claim: Binding of target RNA results in subtle conformational changes in the effector complex.
source: Binding of this 'target RNA' results in subtle conformational changes in the effector complex, activating the catalytic Cas10 subunit which uses its HD-nuclease domain to degrade DNA (Elmore et al., 2016; Estrella et al., 2016; Kazlauskiene et al., 2016; Jung et al., 2015; Han et al., 2017b) and its cyclase domain to synthesise cyclic oligoadenylate (cOA) molecules by polymerisation of ATP (Kazlauskiene et al., 2017; Niewoehner et al., 2017; Rouillon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Cas10 uses its HD-nuclease domain to degrade DNA.
source: Binding of this 'target RNA' results in subtle conformational changes in the effector complex, activating the catalytic Cas10 subunit which uses its HD-nuclease domain to degrade DNA (Elmore et al., 2016; Estrella et al., 2016; Kazlauskiene et al., 2016; Jung et al., 2015; Han et al., 2017b) and its cyclase domain to synthesise cyclic oligoadenylate (cOA) molecules by polymerisation of ATP (Kazlauskiene et al., 2017; Niewoehner et al., 2017; Rouillon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cas10 uses its cyclase domain to synthesize cyclic oligoadenylate (cOA) molecules by polymerization of ATP.
source: Binding of this 'target RNA' results in subtle conformational changes in the effector complex, activating the catalytic Cas10 subunit which uses its HD-nuclease domain to degrade DNA (Elmore et al., 2016; Estrella et al., 2016; Kazlauskiene et al., 2016; Jung et al., 2015; Han et al., 2017b) and its cyclase domain to synthesise cyclic oligoadenylate (cOA) molecules by polymerisation of ATP (Kazlauskiene et al., 2017; Niewoehner et al., 2017; Rouillon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cyclic oligoadenylate molecules range from 3 to 6 AMP monomers in size (cA3 to cA6).
source: These cyclic molecules, which range from 3 to 6 AMP monomers in size (cA3 to cA6), act as second messengers in the cell, signalling viral infection and activating cellular defences.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cOA diversity.

claim: cA4 and cA6 bind specifically to two subtypes of CRISPR Associated Rossman Fold (CARF) domain.
source: cA4 and cA6 bind specifically to two subtypes of CRISPR Associated Rossman Fold (CARF) domain (Makarova et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Makarova et al., 2014.

claim: CARF domains are fused to a range of effector domains that carry out defensive duties.
source: These domains are fused to a range of effector domains that carry out defensive duties.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CARF domain architecture.

claim: The Csx1/Csm6 family utilizes a C-terminal HEPN domain to cleave RNA non-specifically.
source: The best characterised is the Csx1/Csm6 family that utilises a C-terminal HEPN (Higher Eukaryotes and Prokaryotes, Nucleotide binding) domain to cleave RNA non-specifically (Niewoehner and Jinek, 2016; Sheppard et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Csx1/Csm6 ancillary ribonucleases are crucial for CRISPR-based immunity in vivo in several different organisms.
source: The Csx1/Csm6 ancillary ribonucleases are crucial for CRISPR-based immunity in vivo in several different organisms, emphasizing the importance of cOA signalling for type III CRISPR defence (Jiang et al., 2016; Grüschow et al., 2019; Foster et al., 2019; Deng et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to in vivo studies.

claim: Can1 is a cA4-activated DNA nickase present in Thermus thermophilus.
source: A wide variety of alternative CARF-domain proteins associated with type III CRISPR loci have been identified but not yet described (Shmakov et al., 2018; Shah et al., 2019), and recent work has characterized the cA4-activated DNA nickase Can1, which is present in Thermus thermophilus (McMahon et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McMahon et al., 2020.

claim: Activation of the anti-viral state generates collateral damage to host nucleic acids.
source: However, activation of this anti-viral state is known to generate collateral damage to host nucleic acids (Rostøl and Marraffini, 2019) that could lead to dormancy or cell death.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rostøl and Marraffini, 2019.

claim: The cOA-signalling pathway needs a mechanism to remove cOA molecules if a viral infection can be cleared.
source: While this could be an acceptable outcome for an infected cell, if a viral infection can be cleared then the cOA-signalling pathway needs a mechanism to remove the cOA molecules and return the cell to a basal state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the need to return cells to a basal state after infection.

claim: Some archaea encode a dedicated ring nuclease named Crn1.
source: Some archaea encode a dedicated ring nuclease (Athukoralage et al., 2018), recently named as the Crn1 family (CRISPR-associated ring nuclease 1) (Athukoralage et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Crn1 splits the cA4 ring into two linear A2 products to switch off the antiviral response.
source: Crn1 is a specialised CARF domain protein that splits the cA4 ring into two linear A2 products to switch off the antiviral response (Athukoralage et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Athukoralage et al., 2018.

claim: The CARF domains of Csx1/Csm6 family nucleases slowly degrade cOA, acting as bi-functional, self-limiting nucleases.
source: In other systems, the CARF domains of Csx1/Csm6 family nucleases slowly degrade cOA, thus acting as bi-functional, self-limiting nucleases (Athukoralage et al., 2019; Jia et al., 2019; Garcia-Doval et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Many archaeal viruses and some bacteriophage encode a specialized ring nuclease as an anti-CRISPR.
source: Many archaeal viruses and some bacteriophage also encode a specialised ring nuclease as an anti-CRISPR (Acr).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: AcrIII-1 binds cA4 by means of a distinct protein fold (DUF1874) unrelated to the CARF domain.
source: This enzyme, known as AcrIII-1, binds cA4 by means of a distinct protein fold (DUF1874) unrelated to the CARF domain, and degrades cA4 rapidly using conserved active site residues (Athukoralage et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Athukoralage et al., 2020a.

claim: AcrIII-1 degrades cA4 rapidly using conserved active site residues.
source: This enzyme, known as AcrIII-1, binds cA4 by means of a distinct protein fold (DUF1874) unrelated to the CARF domain, and degrades cA4 rapidly using conserved active site residues (Athukoralage et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Athukoralage et al., 2020a.

claim: Viral ring nucleases can abrogate type III CRISPR immunity by rapidly destroying the cA4 infection signal.
source: These viral ring nucleases can abrogate type III CRISPR immunity by rapidly destroying the cA4 infection signal.
evidence: This is supported by citations and experimental evidence.

claim: AcrIII-1 has been co-opted into some bacterial type III CRISPR systems and named Crn2.
source: This enzyme has been co-opted into some bacterial type III CRISPR systems, where it likely acts to degrade cA4 following clearance of phage infection. In this context, it has been named as CRISPR-associated ring nuclease 2 (Crn2) (Athukoralage et al., 2020a; Samolygo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Csx3 from Archaeoglobus fulgidus has been described as an RNA deadenylation enzyme.
source: Csx3 from Archaeoglobus fulgidus has been described as an RNA deadenylation enzyme and crystallised in complex with a pseudo-symmetric RNA tetraloop (Yan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yan et al., 2015.

claim: Structural analysis suggested that Csx3 may be a distantly related member of the CARF family of proteins.
source: Subsequent structural analysis suggested that the Csx3 protein may be a distantly related member of the CARF family of proteins (Topuzlu and Lawrence, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Topuzlu and Lawrence, 2016.

claim: Csx3 is found associated with many type III CRISPR systems.
source: Here, we focus on the Csx3 family of proteins, which is found associated with many type III CRISPR systems (Shah et al., 2019; Shmakov et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shah et al., 2019 and Shmakov et al., 2018.

claim: Csx3 binds cyclic tetra-adenylate with an apparent dissociation constant <0.1 µM.
source: Initial studies showed that Csx3 binds cyclic tetra-adenylate with an apparent dissociation constant <0.1 µM.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: An RNA oligonucleotide (49-9A) with a 9A poly-adenylate 3' tail bound 100-fold less tightly than cA4, with an apparent dissociation constant around 10 µM.
source: In contrast, an RNA oligonucleotide (49-9A) with a 9A poly-adenylate 3' tail bound 100-fold less tightly, with an apparent dissociation constant around 10 µM (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Csx3 cleaves RNA substrate 49-9A in the presence of Mn2+ ions, removing nucleotides from the 3' end.
source: Csx3 cleaved this substrate in the presence of Mn2+ ions, removing nucleotides from the 3' end (Figure 2A), in keeping with previous observations (Yan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and citation to Yan et al., 2015.

claim: Csx3 cleaved cA4 with a far higher rate than RNA.
source: However, Csx3 cleaved cA4 with a far higher rate (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The single-turnover rate constant for RNA cleavage by Csx3 is 0.0063 ± 0.0013 min−1.
source: The single-turnover rate constants were determined as 0.0063 ± 0.0013 min−1 for RNA and 3.5 ± 0.16 min−1 for cA4 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The single-turnover rate constant for cA4 cleavage by Csx3 is 3.5 ± 0.16 min−1.
source: The single-turnover rate constants were determined as 0.0063 ± 0.0013 min−1 for RNA and 3.5 ± 0.16 min−1 for cA4 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Csx3 cleaves cA4 approximately 600-fold faster than RNA.
source: The ~600 fold faster cleavage rate for cA4 compared to RNA strongly suggests that cA4 is the physiological substrate, and that RNA with a 3' polyA tail represents a substrate analogue of the cyclic nucleotide, as observed previously for a Csx1/Csm6 family enzyme (Han et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is calculated from the rate constants and supported by experimental data.

claim: cA4 is the physiological substrate of Csx3.
source: The ~600 fold faster cleavage rate for cA4 compared to RNA strongly suggests that cA4 is the physiological substrate, and that RNA with a 3' polyA tail represents a substrate analogue of the cyclic nucleotide, as observed previously for a Csx1/Csm6 family enzyme (Han et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is inferred from the much higher cleavage rate for cA4 compared to RNA.

claim: The products of the cA4 cleavage reaction are predominantly linear di-adenylate (A2P), plus a small amount of A2P with a cyclic phosphate (A2>P).
source: The products of the cA4 cleavage reaction were identified by liquid-chromatography high-resolution mass spectrometry (LC-HRMS) as predominantly linear di-adenylate (A2P), plus a small amount of A2P with a cyclic phosphate (A2 >P) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by LC-HRMS data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: There are two active sites in the dimeric Csx3 structure.
source: This suggests there are two active sites in the dimeric Csx3 structure, as seen for the ring nuclease Crn1 (Athukoralage et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the cleavage products and comparison to Crn1.

claim: Csx3 from Methanosarcina mazei shows similar cA4 cleavage activity to A. fulgidus Csx3.
source: Similar results were obtained for Csx3 from the mesophilic archaeon Methanosarcina mazei (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Csx1 provided significant immunity (three logs) against plasmid transformation when a targeting crRNA specific for the plasmid was provided.
source: Csx1 provided significant immunity (three logs) against plasmid transformation when a targeting crRNA specific for the plasmid was provided (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: AcrIII-1 from bacteriophage THSA-485A abolished immunity mediated by cA4.
source: As a control, we added the phage ring nuclease AcrIII-1 from bacteriophage THSA-485A, which we previously showed could abolish immunity mediated by cA4 (Athukoralage et al., 2020a), and observed the expected loss of plasmid targeting, reflected in higher transformation efficiencies.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to Athukoralage et al., 2020a.

claim: M. mazei Csx3 caused smaller but significant increases in plasmid transformation efficiency compared to AcrIII-1.
source: When the phage ring nuclease gene was replaced by a gene encoding Csx3 from M. mazei (chosen as the organism grows at close to 37°C, in common with E. coli) we observed smaller but significant increases in plasmid transformation efficiency, with an effect that increased from 18 to 40 hr growth post-transformation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The effect of M. mazei Csx3 on plasmid transformation efficiency increased from 18 to 40 hr growth post-transformation.
source: When the phage ring nuclease gene was replaced by a gene encoding Csx3 from M. mazei (chosen as the organism grows at close to 37°C, in common with E. coli) we observed smaller but significant increases in plasmid transformation efficiency, with an effect that increased from 18 to 40 hr growth post-transformation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The observations with M. mazei Csx3 were consistent with a partial deactivation of the Csx1 ribonuclease due to degradation of cA4.
source: These observations were consistent with a partial deactivation of the Csx1 ribonuclease due to degradation of cA4 by the Csx3 enzyme.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: Csx3 functions as part of the type III CRISPR defence in cells that express it.
source: The effect is not as striking as when using a bona fide Acr protein, which is consistent with the prediction that Csx3 functions as part of the type III CRISPR defence in cells that express it – rather than an Acr.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of Csx3 and AcrIII-1 effects.

claim: The presence of manganese ions is required for the cA4 cleavage activity of Csx3.
source: We tested the metal ion dependence of the cA4 cleavage activity and confirmed that the presence of Mn2+ or Co2+ ions was required for catalysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The presence of cobalt ions is required for the cA4 cleavage activity of Csx3.
source: We tested the metal ion dependence of the cA4 cleavage activity and confirmed that the presence of Mn2+ or Co2+ ions was required for catalysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The H60A variant of Csx3 lacks any detectable catalytic activity.
source: We recapitulated the H60A variant and found that, in agreement with the previous study, the variant lacked any detectable catalytic activity (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and citation to Yan et al., 2015.

claim: H60 and the presumed metal binding site are essential for the ring nuclease activity of Csx3.
source: Thus, it appears that H60 and the presumed metal binding site are essential for the ring nuclease activity of Csx3 despite being situated on the opposite face of the Csx3 dimer, over 20 Å away from the cA4 binding site.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of activity in the H60A variant.

claim: H60 is situated on the opposite face of the Csx3 dimer, over 20 Å away from the cA4 binding site.
source: Thus, it appears that H60 and the presumed metal binding site are essential for the ring nuclease activity of Csx3 despite being situated on the opposite face of the Csx3 dimer, over 20 Å away from the cA4 binding site.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: D69 is a conserved aspartate residue positioned adjacent (~4 Å) to the bound RNA in the crystal structure.
source: Examination of the multiple sequence alignment of Csx3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) revealed the presence of a conserved aspartate residue, D69, which is positioned adjacent (~4 Å) to the bound RNA in the crystal structure (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment and structural data.

claim: The D69A variant of Csx3 was completely catalytically inactive as a ring nuclease.
source: The D69A variant was completely catalytically inactive as a ring nuclease, confirming the importance of D69 in the catalytic mechanism and suggesting that catalysis requires residues on both faces of the dimer (henceforth denoted as the 'D69 face' and 'H60 face').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Catalysis by Csx3 requires residues on both faces of the dimer.
source: The D69A variant was completely catalytically inactive as a ring nuclease, confirming the importance of D69 in the catalytic mechanism and suggesting that catalysis requires residues on both faces of the dimer (henceforth denoted as the 'D69 face' and 'H60 face').
evidence: This is inferred from the inactivity of both H60A and D69A variants.

claim: Csx3 has a shared active site that is formed when two dimers come together, forming a tetramer.
source: A possible explanation for this was that Csx3 has a shared active site that is formed when two dimers come together, forming a tetramer.
evidence: This is inferred from the requirement for residues on both faces of the dimer.

claim: Ring nuclease activity was recovered when the two inactive variants H60A and D69A were mixed together.
source: Accordingly, we took the two inactive variants of Csx3, H60A and D69A, and tested their ring nuclease activity when mixed together (Figure 4B). Ring nuclease activity was recovered when the two inactive variants were combined.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The recovery of activity when mixing H60A and D69A variants supports the hypothesis that the reaction mechanism involves two half-sites that combine to form a single active site bridging two dimers.
source: This result was strongly supportive of the hypothesis that the reaction mechanism involves two half-sites that combine to form a single active site that bridges two dimers of the enzyme.
evidence: This is inferred from the complementation experiment.

claim: The H60A variant of Csx3 was crystallized and the structure was solved to 1.84 Å resolution.
source: In parallel with the biochemical analysis, we crystallised the H60A variant of Csx3 and soaked the cA4 substrate into the crystals. The structure was solved using molecular replacement with data to 1.84 Å resolution (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data.

claim: The electron density clearly showed a molecule of cA4 bound between adjacent dimers of Csx3.
source: The electron density clearly showed a molecule of cA4 bound between adjacent dimers of Csx3 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The Csx3 structure crystallized in a different space group than previously published structures.
source: Notably, the Csx3 structure presented here crystallised in a different space group to those structures published previously (Yan et al., 2015), which has allowed the arrangement of Csx3 dimers into a pseudo filament arrangement (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) with a cA4 molecule sandwiched between the D69 and H60 faces of the protein.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data and comparison to prior structures.

claim: Csx3 dimers arrange into a pseudo filament arrangement with cA4 molecules sandwiched between the D69 and H60 faces.
source: Notably, the Csx3 structure presented here crystallised in a different space group to those structures published previously (Yan et al., 2015), which has allowed the arrangement of Csx3 dimers into a pseudo filament arrangement (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) with a cA4 molecule sandwiched between the D69 and H60 faces of the protein.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The rotation between adjacent dimers in the Csx3 filament is 144°, coupled with a translation of 28 Å.
source: The rotation between adjacent dimers in the filament is 144 °, coupled with a translation of 28 Å.
evidence: This is calculated from the crystal structure.

claim: The interface of the two monomers forming the Csx3 dimer is around 1020 Å2.
source: The interface of the two monomers forming the dimer is around 1020 Å2.
evidence: This is calculated from the crystal structure.

claim: The interface area between the D69 face and cA4 is around 940 Å2 (470 Å2 per monomer).
source: The interface area between the D69 face, which forms the majority of the interactions with cA4, is around 940 Å2 (470 Å2 per monomer), and for the H60 face is around 340 Å2 (170 Å2 per monomer).
evidence: This is calculated from the crystal structure.

claim: The interface area between the H60 face and cA4 is around 340 Å2 (170 Å2 per monomer).
source: The interface area between the D69 face, which forms the majority of the interactions with cA4, is around 940 Å2 (470 Å2 per monomer), and for the H60 face is around 340 Å2 (170 Å2 per monomer).
evidence: This is calculated from the crystal structure.

claim: There is a buried surface area of around 700 Å2 (350 Å2 per monomer) between two adjacent Csx3 dimers.
source: Interestingly, although not annotated as a tetramer, there is a buried surface area of around 700 Å2 (350 Å2 per monomer) between the two adjacent dimers.
evidence: This is calculated from the crystal structure.

claim: There are no significant conformational changes or large loop movements upon cA4 binding to Csx3.
source: From comparison to the apo Csx3 structure, we hypothesize there are no significant conformational changes or large loop movements upon binding, but instead suggest subtle movements of active site and interacting residues to accommodate cA4.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of apo and cA4-bound structures.

claim: The majority of interactions with cA4 are made by the D69 face of Csx3.
source: The majority of interactions are made by the D69 face.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5B,C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: cA4 hydrogen bonds with the main chain atoms of I22, S44, G45, and I49 in Csx3.
source: The cA4 hydrogen bonds with the main chain atoms of I22, S44, G45, and I49, and side chain atoms of S44, R46 and R71 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: cA4 hydrogen bonds with the side chain atoms of S44, R46 and R71 in Csx3.
source: The cA4 hydrogen bonds with the main chain atoms of I22, S44, G45, and I49, and side chain atoms of S44, R46 and R71 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Residues G45, I49, and R71 are absolutely conserved in the Csx3 family.
source: Despite the number of main chain interactions, these residues are either absolutely (G45, I49, and R71) or highly (I22, S44 and R46) conserved (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Residues I22, S44 and R46 are highly conserved in the Csx3 family.
source: Despite the number of main chain interactions, these residues are either absolutely (G45, I49, and R71) or highly (I22, S44 and R46) conserved (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: H80 forms a strong (2.4–2.5 Å) hydrogen bond with the 2'-OH of the ribose ring of cA4.
source: The one interaction evident from the H60 face with cA4 is a strong (2.4–2.5 Å) hydrogen bond between H80 and the 2'-OH of the ribose ring.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: H60, H80, and H57 are all absolutely conserved in the Csx3 family.
source: H60, H80, and another histidine residue (H57) nearby on the H60 face are all absolutely conserved in the Csx3 family (Figure 5B,C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ribose of each AMP moiety of cA4 adopts a relaxed 2'-endo conformation.
source: The ribose of each AMP moiety of cA4 adopts a relaxed 2'-endo conformation, with the four adenine bases each filling a pocket.
evidence: This is supported by structural data.

claim: There is plasticity around the base recognition sites of Csx3.
source: Given the Csx3 structure in complex with an RNA fragment (Yan et al., 2015) had two adenine, one uracil and one guanine bases in the same position as the four adenine bases described here, there is obviously some plasticity around these recognition sites.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with the RNA-bound structure.

claim: R71 moves around 3.3 Å to form bidentate hydrogen bonds with an oxygen atom of a phosphate group adjacent to the phosphodiester bond that is cleaved.
source: Interestingly, R71 moves around 3.3 Å in order to form bidentate hydrogen bonds with an oxygen atom of a phosphate group, which we predict is adjacent to the phosphodiester bond that is cleaved (Figure 5C and text below).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The movement of R71 brings it within hydrogen bonding distance of D69.
source: This movement of R71 brings it within hydrogen bonding distance of D69, which has been shown to be vital for activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: H80 moves around 3.3 Å to hydrogen bond with cA4.
source: The position of H80 also differs between the two structures; the residue moves around 3.3 Å in order to hydrogen bond with the cA4.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: H60 and H57 are the most likely candidates for coordinating metal ions in Csx3.
source: There are a number of histidine residues in or near the active site which could be involved in coordinating one or more Mn2+ ions (Figure 5—figure supplement 4). H60 and H57 are the most likely candidates; they are both absolutely conserved, and the position of the alanine residue in the H60A variant structure suggests this residue does not move significantly upon tetramer formation.
evidence: This is inferred from structural data and conservation patterns.

claim: The position of H57 is identical in the apo and cA4-bound structures.
source: The position of H57 is identical in the apo and cA4-bound structures.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison.

claim: It is feasible that one or both H60 and/or H57 residues coordinate one or more metal ions.
source: It is therefore feasible that one or both H60 and/or H57 residues coordinate one or more metal ions, and there is the possibility that just one metal ion bridges the two monomers.
evidence: This is speculative based on structural data.

claim: The best candidate phosphodiester bond for cleavage has an angle of 152° between the 2'-OH, P and O moieties.
source: The other ring nucleases characterised to date are metal independent enzymes that are predicted to work by catalysing in-line nucleophilic attack by a 2'-hydroxyl group of the cA4 substrate on an adjacent phosphodiester bond. In this regard, the best candidate for cleavage is the P-O bond of the phosphate (labelled *), as the angle formed between the 2'-OH, P and O moieties is 152° (Figure 5C), which although lower to that seen for the ring nuclease AcrIII-1 (Athukoralage et al., 2020a), is still significantly higher than the angle (129°) between the same atoms in both adjacent adenine moieties.
evidence: This is calculated from the crystal structure.

claim: R71 may participate in stabilization of the transition state or oxyanion leaving group.
source: The absolutely conserved residue R71 interacts with this phosphate group via a bidentate hydrogen bond and may participate in stabilisation of the transition state or oxyanion leaving group.
evidence: This is speculative based on structural data.

claim: D69 and R71 may serve to position each other correctly and/or perturb their respective pKa's to enhance catalysis.
source: The conserved catalytic residue D69 in turn makes polar contacts with R71. These two residues may serve to position each other correctly (and/or perturb their respective pKa's) to enhance catalysis.
evidence: This is speculative based on structural data.

claim: H80 may play a 'pinning' role to ensure engagement of the H60 face in catalysis.
source: The conserved H80 residue forms a hydrogen bond with the cA4. As it is one of only two residues from the H60 face that interacts with cA4, H80 may play a 'pinning' role to ensure engagement of the H60 face in catalysis.
evidence: This is speculative based on structural data.

claim: Csx3 variants R71A and H80A both displayed highly reduced ring nuclease activity.
source: Csx3 variants R71A and H80A both displayed highly reduced ring nuclease activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 5), consistent with important roles in cA4 binding and/or catalysis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: The primary product of cA4 cleavage by Csx3 is A2P rather than A2>P.
source: The observations that Mn2+ is required for catalysis, and that the primary product of cA4 cleavage is A2P rather than A2>P (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1) are suggestive (but not diagnostic) of a mechanism whereby a metal-activated hydroxyl ion initiates nucleophilic attack on the phosphodiester bond (Yang, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The observations that Mn2+ is required and A2P is the primary product are suggestive of a mechanism whereby a metal-activated hydroxyl ion initiates nucleophilic attack on the phosphodiester bond.
source: The observations that Mn2+ is required for catalysis, and that the primary product of cA4 cleavage is A2P rather than A2>P (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1) are suggestive (but not diagnostic) of a mechanism whereby a metal-activated hydroxyl ion initiates nucleophilic attack on the phosphodiester bond (Yang, 2011).
evidence: This is speculative based on experimental data and citation.

claim: The metal independent ring nuclease AcrIII-1 largely generates A2P, presumably due to rapid hydrolysis of the cyclic phosphate following phosphodiester bond cleavage.
source: Uncertainty arises from the observation that the metal independent ring nuclease AcrIII-1 also largely generates A2P, presumably due to the rapid hydrolysis of the cyclic phosphate following phosphodiester bond cleavage (Athukoralage et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Athukoralage et al., 2020a.

claim: H57 and H60 are in appropriate positions to contribute to catalysis by coordination of the essential catalytic Mn2+ ion(s).
source: The conserved histidine residues H57 and H60 are in appropriate positions to contribute to catalysis by coordination of the essential catalytic Mn2+ ion(s).
evidence: This is inferred from structural data.

claim: The inactive H60A variant of Csx3 had a milky, colloidal property on addition of cA4.
source: In support of this model, we observed that the inactive H60A variant of Csx3 had a milky, colloidal property on addition of cA4, which we interpreted as being due to the formation of long Csx3 fibres bridged by multiple cA4 molecules (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The milky, colloidal property of H60A Csx3 with cA4 is due to the formation of long Csx3 fibres bridged by multiple cA4 molecules.
source: In support of this model, we observed that the inactive H60A variant of Csx3 had a milky, colloidal property on addition of cA4, which we interpreted as being due to the formation of long Csx3 fibres bridged by multiple cA4 molecules (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation.

claim: Wild-type Csx3 did not show colloidal behavior with cA4, presumably because cA4 was rapidly cleaved.
source: The wild-type protein did not show this behaviour, presumably because cA4 was rapidly cleaved.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation.

claim: The addition of cA4 to Csx3 resulted in mixed oligomeric species with significantly increased particle size and molecular weight.
source: We confirmed the propensity of Csx3 to oligomerise upon cA4 addition by dynamic light scattering (DLS) measurements in buffer devoid of metal ions. Under these conditions, the addition of cA4 resulted in mixed oligomeric species with significantly increased particle size and molecular weight, whereas the molecular weight of particles formed in the absence of cA4 were consistent with homodimers of Csx3 (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by DLS data shown in Supplementary file 2.

claim: In the absence of cA4, the molecular weight of Csx3 particles were consistent with homodimers.
source: We confirmed the propensity of Csx3 to oligomerise upon cA4 addition by dynamic light scattering (DLS) measurements in buffer devoid of metal ions. Under these conditions, the addition of cA4 resulted in mixed oligomeric species with significantly increased particle size and molecular weight, whereas the molecular weight of particles formed in the absence of cA4 were consistent with homodimers of Csx3 (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by DLS data shown in Supplementary file 2.

claim: A plot of initial velocity against enzyme concentration revealed a sigmoidal relationship that could be fitted to the Hill equation with a Hill coefficient of 1.8.
source: A plot of initial velocity against [E] revealed a sigmoidal relationship that could be fitted to the Hill equation with a Hill coefficient of 1.8 (Figure 6), consistent with obligate dimerization (of Csx3 dimers) in the reaction cycle.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The Hill coefficient of 1.8 is consistent with obligate dimerization of Csx3 dimers in the reaction cycle.
source: A plot of initial velocity against [E] revealed a sigmoidal relationship that could be fitted to the Hill equation with a Hill coefficient of 1.8 (Figure 6), consistent with obligate dimerization (of Csx3 dimers) in the reaction cycle.
evidence: This is inferred from the Hill coefficient value.

claim: The cooperativity of Csx3 may be important to modulate ring nuclease activity appropriately in the cell, particularly if the concentration of Csx3 changes in response to viral infection.
source: Practically, this cooperativity may be important to modulate the ring nuclease activity of Csx3 appropriately in the cell, particularly if the concentration of Csx3 changes in response to viral infection.
evidence: This is speculative based on the cooperative kinetics data.

claim: The maximal multiple turnover rate constant for Csx3 was 0.075 min−1 at 70°C.
source: The maximal multiple turnover rate constant observed under these conditions was 0.075 min−1 at 70°C, about 50-fold lower than the rate for the chemical step of catalysis measured under single turnover conditions at 50°C.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The multiple turnover rate constant is about 50-fold lower than the rate for the chemical step of catalysis measured under single turnover conditions.
source: The maximal multiple turnover rate constant observed under these conditions was 0.075 min−1 at 70°C, about 50-fold lower than the rate for the chemical step of catalysis measured under single turnover conditions at 50°C.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data.

claim: The association of Csx3 dimers sandwiching cA4, or the dissociation of the complex following product formation, limits the turnover number of the enzyme significantly.
source: Thus, the association of Csx3 dimers sandwiching cA4, or the dissociation of the complex following product formation, limits the turnover number of the enzyme significantly.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of single and multiple turnover rates.

claim: Csx3 binds much more tightly to cA4 than to RNA.
source: While we confirmed the main experimental observations of the original study (Yan et al., 2015), our analyses have revealed that Csx3 binds much more tightly to cA4 than to RNA, is considerably more active as a cA4-specific ring nuclease than an RNA deadenylase, and has properties consistent with a function as a ring nuclease in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Csx3 is considerably more active as a cA4-specific ring nuclease than an RNA deadenylase.
source: While we confirmed the main experimental observations of the original study (Yan et al., 2015), our analyses have revealed that Csx3 binds much more tightly to cA4 than to RNA, is considerably more active as a cA4-specific ring nuclease than an RNA deadenylase, and has properties consistent with a function as a ring nuclease in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Csx3 has properties consistent with a function as a ring nuclease in vivo.
source: While we confirmed the main experimental observations of the original study (Yan et al., 2015), our analyses have revealed that Csx3 binds much more tightly to cA4 than to RNA, is considerably more active as a cA4-specific ring nuclease than an RNA deadenylase, and has properties consistent with a function as a ring nuclease in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Csx3 functions as a cA4-specific ring nuclease in type III CRISPR systems.
source: These data indicate that Csx3 functions as a cA4-specific ring nuclease in type III CRISPR systems.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the manuscript, supported by all experimental data.

claim: The Crn1 family of ring nucleases was originally identified in the Sulfolobales and related crenarchaea.
source: The Crn1 family of ring nucleases, based on the CARF domain fold, was originally identified in the Sulfolobales and related crenarchaea (Athukoralage et al., 2018), where their function is thought to be to remove cA4 from the cell once a viral infection has been cleared.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Athukoralage et al., 2018.

claim: The function of Crn1 is thought to be to remove cA4 from the cell once a viral infection has been cleared.
source: The Crn1 family of ring nucleases, based on the CARF domain fold, was originally identified in the Sulfolobales and related crenarchaea (Athukoralage et al., 2018), where their function is thought to be to remove cA4 from the cell once a viral infection has been cleared.
evidence: This is supported by citation and inference.

claim: Homologues of AcrIII-1 are found associated with some bacterial type III CRISPR systems and have been named Crn2.
source: Homologues of AcrIII-1 are also found associated with some bacterial type III CRISPR systems, and in this context have been named as CRISPR associated ring nuclease 2 (Crn2) enzymes (Athukoralage et al., 2020a; Samolygo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Ring nuclease activity has been identified associated with the CARF domains of some Csx1/Csm6 family ribonucleases, which are bifunctional, self-limiting CRISPR ancillary defence enzymes.
source: Ring nuclease activity has also been identified associated with the CARF domains of some Csx1/Csm6 family ribonucleases, which are therefore bifunctional, self-limiting CRISPR ancillary defence enzymes (Jia et al., 2019; Athukoralage et al., 2019; Garcia-Doval et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cells with a type III CRISPR defence require a mechanism to remove the cOA signal.
source: It appears to be an emerging paradigm that cells with a type III CRISPR defence require a mechanism to remove the cOA signal, either once viral infection is cleared, or when the system 'fires' inappropriately due to self-targeting (Athukoralage et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by citation and inference from the data.

claim: A. fulgidus Crn3/Csx3 is a much faster enzyme than Crn1.
source: A. fulgidus Crn3/Csx3 is a much faster enzyme than Crn1.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of rate constants.

claim: The single turnover reaction rate for cA4 cleavage by Crn3/Csx3 of 3.6 min−1 is closer to that of the AcrIII-1 family.
source: The single turnover reaction rate for cA4 cleavage of 3.6 min−1 is closer to that of the AcrIII-1 family, which utilises a distinct active site architecture, employing a conserved histidine residue as a general acid to stabilise the oxyanion leaving group (Athukoralage et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to cited data.

claim: Crn3/Csx3 functions via a highly unusual cooperative mechanism where two enzyme dimers associate to sandwich a cA4 substrate molecule.
source: A key observation is that Crn3/Csx3 functions via a highly unusual cooperative mechanism where two enzyme dimers associate to sandwich a cA4 substrate molecule.
evidence: This is supported by structural and biochemical data.

claim: The active site of Crn3/Csx3 is composed of two half-sites that are present on opposite faces of each dimeric moiety.
source: The active site is thus composed of two half-sites that are present on opposite faces of each dimeric moiety, with enzyme tetramers formed transiently to complete the catalytic cycle.
evidence: This is supported by structural and biochemical data.

claim: Enzyme tetramers are formed transiently to complete the catalytic cycle of Crn3/Csx3.
source: The active site is thus composed of two half-sites that are present on opposite faces of each dimeric moiety, with enzyme tetramers formed transiently to complete the catalytic cycle.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and biochemical data.

claim: The substrate-induced, non-allosteric, dimerization of Csx3 appears unprecedented in the literature.
source: However, the substrate-induced, non-allosteric, dimerization of Csx3 appears unprecedented in the literature – a partial exception being the example of the Arginine Finger of AAA+ ATPases (Nagy et al., 2016), where interdomain interactions with ATP can influence quaternary structure (Zhao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from literature comparison.

claim: Cooperative kinetics of Crn3/Csx3 result in low concentrations providing very low levels of ring nuclease activity that rapidly increases with increasing enzyme concentrations.
source: This results in cooperative kinetics where low concentrations of Crn3/Csx3 provide very low levels of ring nuclease activity that rapidly increases with increasing enzyme concentrations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The rate of cA4 turnover by Crn3/Csx3 is limited by the formation of protein:cA4 complexes or dissociation of the products, rather than the catalytic step.
source: Furthermore, the rate of cA4 turnover is limited by the formation of protein:cA4 complexes or dissociation of the products, rather than the catalytic step, which is significantly faster.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of single and multiple turnover rates.

claim: The cooperative mechanism of Crn3/Csx3 may provide a means to control ring nuclease activity in an appropriate manner to ensure that cA4 activation of ancillary ribonucleases is allowed to proceed and provide immunity.
source: Together, these factors may provide a means to control ring nuclease activity in an appropriate manner thus ensuring that cA4 activation of ancillary ribonucleases is allowed to proceed and provide immunity.
evidence: This is speculative based on the kinetic data.

claim: Alterations in the gene expression levels of Csx3 would have a large effect on the overall rate of catalysis.
source: Thus, alterations in the gene expression levels of Csx3 would have a large effect on the overall rate of catalysis.
evidence: This is inferred from the cooperative kinetics.

claim: The observed specificity of Crn3/Csx3 for cA4 implicates the corresponding type III CRISPR systems as functioning via a cA4 second messenger.
source: Finally, the observed specificity of Crn3/Csx3 for cA4 implicates the corresponding type III CRISPR systems as functioning via a cA4 second messenger.
evidence: This is inferred from the substrate specificity data.

claim: cA4 is the default cyclic nucleotide employed to signal infection and activate defences in type III CRISPR systems.
source: Although this conclusion may be influenced by a sampling bias, it appears that cA4 is the default cyclic nucleotide employed to signal infection and activate defences in type III CRISPR systems.
evidence: This is inferred from the data and literature.

claim: It is possible that the pressure applied by cA4-specific anti-CRISPRs has resulted in the utilization of cA3 and cA6 second messengers in some bacterial defence systems.
source: It is possible that the pressure applied by cA4-specific anti-CRISPRs has resulted in the utilization of cA3 and cA6 second messengers in some bacterial defence systems.
evidence: This is speculative.

claim: Csx3 is most commonly observed in the euryarchaea and cyanobacteria.
source: Csx3 is most commonly observed in the euryarchaea and cyanobacteria (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Csx3 is found next to type III-B CRISPR operons and adjacent to Csx1 and other uncharacterised CARF family proteins.
source: Examination of the genomic context of Csx3 in selected archaeal and bacterial species confirmed its close association with type III-B CRISPR systems and with CARF family proteins such as the ribonuclease Csx1 (Figure 1A), implying a role in cyclic oligoadenylate signalling and providing further impetus to re-examine the function of Csx3.
evidence: This is supported by genomic context data shown in Figure 1A.
